flaws.title: Downward reset skips an initialized start tick, letting zero-for-one reward distribution use too little active liquidity
flaws.sequence:
1. A pool's current tick `t1` is an exact multiple of `tickSpacing` and is an initialized upper boundary, so liquidity in `[t1 - s, t1)` is inactive at the start of a zero-for-one swap.
2. An attacker wins the top-of-block zero-for-one swap that moves the price just below `t1`, while also having liquidity positioned so that it becomes active only after crossing `t1`.
3. `AngstromL2.afterSwap` calls `_zeroForOneDistributeTax`, which builds the downward iterator through `initDown(..., startTick = t1, ...)`, and `reset` sets `currentTick = t1` before immediately calling `_advanceToNextDown`.
4. `_advanceToNextDown` searches from `currentTick - 1`, so the initialized tick `t1` is never returned by `getNext` even though crossing down through `t1` should change active liquidity under Uniswap's `lower <= t < upper` rule.
5. `CompensationPriceFinder.getZeroForOne` and then `_zeroForOneCreditRewards` therefore compute compensation / reward growth using liquidity that omits the liquidity that should have been activated at `t1`.
6. The swap tax is distributed with too small a denominator; in the reward-accounting state used by this code base, that inflated growth can then be claimed by the attacker's position, allowing withdrawal of rewards they were not owed.
flaws.impact: Protocol swap-tax rewards are misallocated. In the known exploit path, an attacker can steal essentially all accumulated rewards from honest LPs.
flaws.known_finding: All rewards can be stolen due to incorrect active liquidity calculations when the current tick is an exact multiple of the tick spacing at the upper end of a liquidity range

flaws.title: Downward reset can make top-of-block zero-for-one swaps revert when they start on an initialized upper boundary
flaws.sequence:
1. An LP has a position `[lower, upper)` where `upper` is an initialized exact multiple of `tickSpacing`, and the pool's current tick is exactly `upper`.
2. A top-of-block zero-for-one swap moves the price down far enough to cross `lower`.
3. `afterSwap` calls `_zeroForOneDistributeTax`, which creates the downward iterator with `startTick = upper`.
4. `reset` leaves `currentTick = upper` and immediately advances downward, so the iterator skips tick `upper` instead of returning it first.
5. The callers start from active liquidity at `upper`, which correctly excludes `[lower, upper)`, but because the skipped `upper` tick is never processed, that position's liquidity is never added when the walk enters `(lower, upper)`.
6. When the iterator later reaches `lower`, `CompensationPriceFinder.getZeroForOne` and `_zeroForOneCreditRewards` execute `liquidity = liquidity.sub(liquidityNet)` with liquidity that is too small, causing an underflow/revert.
7. The revert propagates out of `afterSwap`, reverting the entire swap.
flaws.impact: Certain zero-for-one swaps become unexecutable, denying service to swappers/searchers whenever the swap starts exactly on such a boundary tick.
flaws.known_finding: All rewards can be stolen due to incorrect active liquidity calculations when the current tick is an exact multiple of the tick spacing at the upper end of a liquidity range
